# Package Maintenance and Demos {#chp:maintain}

The last chapter is for people who maintain R packages, and for people who
give talks about them. Both groups have chores that are easy to automate once
somebody writes the function.

## Check reverse dependencies {#sec:rev-check}

The scariest part of releasing a package is wondering whether the new version
breaks packages that depend on it. `rev_check()` runs `R CMD check` on the
reverse dependencies for you. It downloads them, checks them in parallel, and
compares the results against the current CRAN version so that new failures
stand out:

```r
# check all reverse dependencies of knitr, using 4 cores
rev_check("knitr", src = "path/to/knitr_source", n = 4)
```

After the run, `compare_Rcheck()` writes a Markdown diff of only the packages
whose check status changed. You get to focus on regressions rather than old
failures.

## Type code into RStudio for a demo {#sec:rstudio-type}

Pasting code into the editor during a talk looks abrupt. `rstudio_type()` feeds
characters into the RStudio source editor as if a person typed them, which is
nice for live demos and screencasts:

```r
rstudio_type("1 + 1\n", pause = function() 0.05)
```

The `mistake` argument introduces random typos and then fixes them, for an
even more realistic effect.

## Write a bibliography for your packages {#sec:pkg-bib}

Citing the packages you used in a report should not mean typing BibTeX by hand.
`pkg_bib()` turns `citation()` output into entries keyed `R-<package>`:

```{r}
suppressWarnings(pkg_bib("xfun", width = 60))
```

Write to a file with `file = "packages.bib"`, change the key prefix with
`prefix`, or stamp the entries with a retrieval date via `date = "today"`. With
no `x`, it covers all attached packages.

## Bump a version number {#sec:bump-version}

`bump_version()` increases the last component of a version, and works on a
vector:

```{r}
bump_version(c("0.1", "91.2.14", "7.23.9"))
```

## Skip checks for old package versions {#sec:check-old}

When a package breaks under a new R, you may want to skip its tests only while
`R CMD check` runs on an old version of it. These helpers read the package
being checked from the check environment:

```{r}
check_package_name()  # NA outside R CMD check
check_old_package("mypkg", "1.0")  # FALSE outside R CMD check
```

Inside a check of `mypkg`, `check_package_name()` returns `"mypkg"`, and
`check_old_package("mypkg", "1.0")` is `TRUE` if the installed version is `1.0`
or lower. Use it to guard a test:

```r
if (!check_old_package("mypkg", "1.0")) {
  # tests that need version > 1.0
}
```

## Install a package from its source directory {#sec:install-dir}

`install_dir()` runs `R CMD build` and then `R CMD INSTALL`, so vignettes get
built just as they would in a release. Run it from the package root:

```r
install_dir()                 # build a tarball, then install it
install_dir("path/to/pkg", build = FALSE)  # install the directory directly
```

## Reinstall broken packages {#sec:broken-packages}

After upgrading R to a new `x.y` version, installed packages may no longer load.
`broken_packages()` finds them, and reinstalls them by default. Use
`reinstall = FALSE` to only list the culprits:

```r
broken_packages(reinstall = FALSE)  # names of packages that fail to load
broken_packages()                   # find and reinstall them
```

## Check reverse dependencies on GitHub Actions {#sec:crandalf}

If your machine is too slow for `rev_check()` (see @sec:rev-check), push the
job to the [crandalf](https://github.com/yihui/crandalf) repo. Run these inside
a clone of it. `crandalf_check()` splits the reverse dependencies into batches
and pushes one branch per batch to trigger GitHub Actions. `crandalf_results()`
waits for the jobs, then merges and summarizes the results. It needs `git`, and
the GitHub CLI `gh` for the results.

```r
xfun::crandalf_check("knitr", size = 400)
xfun::crandalf_results("knitr")
```

## Upload a package to win-builder {#sec:win-builder}

`upload_win_builder()` builds the package in the current directory and uploads
the tarball to win-builder, which emails you the check results from R-devel,
R-release, and R-oldrelease (pick with `version`). It also runs `git pull` first
when the directory is a Git repo.

```r
xfun::upload_win_builder()
xfun::upload_win_builder(version = "R-devel", server = "https")
```

## Submit a package to CRAN {#sec:submit-cran}

`submit_cran()` builds the package in the current directory and submits it to
CRAN through the web form, using `cran-comments.md` as the comment if it exists.
CRAN then emails you a confirmation link.

```r
xfun::submit_cran()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
This sends your package to CRAN for real. It also syncs the Git branch with the
remote first (`sync = TRUE`). Run `R CMD check --as-cran` and win-builder
first.
:::

## Tag and prepare the next version after a release {#sec:post-release}

Once CRAN accepts a release, `post_release()` does the paperwork: it tags the
release in Git, bumps `DESCRIPTION` to the next dev version (`1.2.3` becomes
`1.2.3.1`), adds a header for the next release to `NEWS.md`, pushes, and creates
a GitHub release from the news items.

```r
xfun::post_release()
```
